aiStories.title: 硅谷AI神童推出Underdog，打造迄今最具隐私性的Instinct与Muse竞品
aiStories.originalTitle: Silicon Valley’s AI wunderkind launches Underdog, the most private Instinct/Muse competitor yet
aiStories.snippet: Sigil Wen, backed by a Silicon Valley who's who, has built an on-device AI assistant that promises to be free, fully private, and capable for everyday tasks.
aiStories.fullContent:
When self-taught coder Sigil Wen was 17, he moved to Silicon Valley and lived in an AI hacker house with famed AI researcher Andrej Karpathy.

While there, he hacked and coded alongside other people who would become the biggest names in AI, like Perplexity founder Aravind Srinivas and OpenAI researcher Noam Brown. He tested early versions of AI tools that would later become well known, including a chatbot shared by Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann that would become Claude, an image generator from David Holz that would become Midjourney, and what would become OpenAI’s GPT-3 and the image generator Stable Diffusion. Prominent investor and entrepreneur Naval Ravikant hired him for Airchat, Ravikant’s now-defunct rival to the Clubhouse social network.

For fun, he figured out how to get GPT-2 running on his Apple Watch. “It was a magical time,” Wen told TechCrunch.

Now a Thiel Fellow — the program from investor Peter Thiel that invites young founders to pursue projects instead of college — Wen on Monday launched an invite-only beta of Underdog, one of the most private AI assistants Silicon Valley has yet to offer. The model runs wholly on-device, meaning the user’s data remains on devices they already own, currently Macs and Windows PCs, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions coming soon.

Underdog is powered by Husky, the inference engine Wen built to run AI models quickly on a user’s own hardware. Wen says it moves less data between a computer’s main chip and its graphics chip than rival on-device engines.

Underdog has other security features baked in, too, like encrypting the keys to the email and other accounts that users authorize Underdog to access.

Underdog is, however, using much smaller models than today’s state-of-the-art ones hosted in data centers. It currently uses a 27-billion parameter reasoning model fine-tuned from Qwen3.8-27B.

Wen argues that this model compares favorably with Claude Opus 4.6 in some benchmarks, or what was considered top performance six months ago. He says that means it can handle the everyday tasks that people want an AI assistant to do, like shopping research or answering math homework questions.

“You don’t need to sacrifice your privacy for the capability because they’re just as capable,” Wen says. He adds that small on-device models will continue to grow more capable over time.

Perhaps the most interesting thing about Underdog is its early business model. The app will be free at first and never ad-supported. Since the AI runs on users’ machines, Underdog doesn’t have the giant overhead of paying a provider for inference. “I don’t have to charge you a subscription to run this because my costs are so super low,” he said.

Instead, with Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison as one of his angel investors, he’s borrowing a play from the fintech era. Underdog will take a tiny percentage of payment transactions that the AI assistant makes using Stripe’s secure payment rails, something like an interchange fee. In this way, the AI assistant never has to mine your data. It is as aligned with you as your bank or credit card providers.

This runs contrary to the business motivations of many of the other players in AI assistants, whose privacy policies allow them to collect data on users that they may sell to advertisers or other third parties, or use to train other models.

That kind of data collection could be a particularly treacherous trade-off for users of an AI assistant, which may need access to the most intimate details about you in order to be useful, from medical conditions to financial data to data on your kids.

As Wen wrote in what he calls his AI manifesto, “Why should using AI require surrendering your private information?”

He tells TechCrunch: “I honestly want to build Underdog for myself. I’m building a product that I would be proud for my future children to use.”

The startup behind Underdog is named Conway Research, and Collison isn’t its only big-name investor. Conway is backed by Andreessen Horowitz via partner Chris Dixon, as well as Khosla Ventures, Hummingbird, SV Angel, the Anthology Fund (the partnership fund between Menlo Ventures and Anthropic), and a prominent list of angel investors that includes Vercel founder Guillermo Rauch, Noam Brown, and Deedy Das, among others.

自学成才的程序员文思齐（Sigil Wen）在17岁时来到硅谷，与著名AI研究员安德烈·卡帕西（Andrej Karpathy）同住在一处AI黑客之家里。

在那里，他与日后成为AI领域赫赫有名的人物并肩编程、钻研技术，包括Perplexity创始人阿拉温德·斯里尼瓦斯（Aravind Srinivas）以及OpenAI研究员诺姆·布朗（Noam Brown）。他测试了日后声名远扬的多款AI工具早期版本，包括Anthropic联合创始人本·曼恩（Ben Mann）分享的聊天机器人（即后来的Claude）、大卫·霍尔茨（David Holz）开发的图像生成器（后来的Midjourney），以及日后演变为OpenAI的GPT-3和图像生成器Stable Diffusion的原型。知名投资人兼创业者纳瓦尔·拉维坎特（Naval Ravikant）还聘请他加入Airchat——拉维坎特旗下面向Clubhouse竞争（现已关停）的社交网络。

为了好玩，他还搞懂了如何在自己的Apple Watch上运行GPT-2。“那是一段不可思议的神奇时光，”文思齐告诉TechCrunch。

如今，文思齐成为了一名蒂尔学者（Thiel Fellow，投资人彼得·蒂尔设立的项目，鼓励年轻创业者辍学创业而非攻读大学）。周一，他推出了Underdog的邀请制内测版，这是硅谷迄今为止隐私性最强的AI助手之一。该模型完全在端侧设备上运行，意味着用户的数据始终留存在其已拥有的设备上，目前支持Mac和Windows PC，Linux、iPhone和Android版本也将很快推出。

Underdog由Husky提供技术支持，这是文思齐自主研发的推理引擎，旨在在用户自有的硬件上高速运行AI模型。文思齐表示，与竞争对手的端侧引擎相比，Husky在电脑主芯片与图形芯片之间传输的数据更少。

Underdog还内置了其他安全功能，例如对用户授权Underdog访问的电子邮件及其他账户的密钥进行加密。

不过，Underdog使用的模型规模远小于当今托管在数据中心的顶尖模型。它目前采用的是一个基于Qwen3.8-27B微调而来的270亿参数推理模型。

文思齐坚称，在某些基准测试中，该模型与Claude Opus 4.6（六个月前的顶尖水平代表）不相上下。他表示，这意味着它能够胜任人们希望AI助手处理的日常任务，比如购物调研或解答数学作业问题。

“你不需要为了获得强大功能而牺牲隐私，因为它们同样能力出众，”文思齐说。他补充道，随着时间推移，小型端侧模型的能力还将持续提升。

也许Underdog最值得关注的地方在于其初期的商业模式。该应用初期将免费提供，并且永远不会投放广告。由于AI是在用户的机器上本地运行，Underdog无需承担向第三方供应商支付推理费用这一庞大开销。“因为我的成本极低，所以我根本不需要向你收取订阅费来运行它，”他说道。

相反，在Stripe联合创始人帕特里克·科利森（Patrick Collison）作为其天使投资人之一的背景下，他借鉴了金融科技时代的打法。当AI助手使用Stripe的安全支付通道进行交易时，Underdog将从中抽取极低比例的交易分成，类似于银行间结算手续费。通过这种方式，AI助手永远不需要挖掘你的数据。它的利益与你的利益保持高度一致，就像你的银行或信用卡发卡行一样。

这与许多其他AI助手玩家的商业动机背道而驰，后者的隐私政策允许其收集用户数据并出售给广告商或其他第三方，或用于训练其他模型。

对于AI助手的用户而言，这种数据收集可能是一种极其危险的妥协，因为AI助手为了发挥作用，可能需要获取你最私密的信息，从身体健康状况到财务数据，再到关于你子女的信息。

正如文思齐在他所谓的“AI宣言”中所写的那样：“为什么使用AI就必须交出你的隐私信息？”

他告诉TechCrunch：“说实话，我是为自己打造Underdog的。我正在做一款能让未来的孩子们自豪使用的产品。”

Underdog背后的初创公司名为Conway Research，科利森并非其唯一的重量级投资人。Conway的投资方还包括由合伙人克里斯·迪克森（Chris Dixon）领衔的Andreessen Horowitz，以及Khosla Ventures、Hummingbird、SV Angel、Anthology Fund（Menlo Ventures与Anthropic联合设立的基金），此外还有豪华的天使投资人阵容，包括Vercel创始人吉列尔莫·劳赫（Guillermo Rauch）、诺姆·布朗（Noam Brown）和迪迪·达斯（Deedy Das）等人。

aiStories.fullContent:

See All Transportation

See All Electric Cars

You can get up to a couple of days of power with the Model 3 or Model Y if you also have Tesla’s Powerwall 3.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

See All by Stevie Bonifield

Some Tesla Model 3 and Model Y owners can use their EV battery to keep the lights on longer during a power outage, now that Tesla’s expanding the Powershare Home Backup feature. It was previously only available on the Cybertruck, and also requires owning Tesla’s Powerwall 3. However, support for the Powerwall 2 and Powerwall Plus is “coming soon.” Tesla’s EVs aren’t the first or only ones with bidirectional charging; companies like Kia and GM also offer vehicle-to-home power on their vehicles, while Nissan’s Leaf offered power-to-grid charging years ago.

Tesla says the Model 3 and Model Y can extend home backup power to over two days for Premium and Performance models, which is shorter than the “over three days” Tesla claims you can get from the Cybertruck’s battery.

As Electrek points out, Tesla is only guaranteeing Home Backup will work on Model 3 and Model Y vehicles ordered from October 1st onward because not all older models include the PCS2 Lite inverter required to make it all work. So far, the feature is also only mentioned as available in the US and Puerto Rico, but not Canada, and not for the larger Model S or Model X. Tesla’s Powershare Grid Support feature is also still exclusive to the Cybertruck.

aiStories.title: AI决策模型如何改变内容审核
aiStories.originalTitle: How AI decision models could change content moderation
aiStories.snippet: On Tuesday, Musubi announced a lightweight decision model made for real-time moderation called PolicyLM-1.7B, released with open weights.
aiStories.fullContent:
As decision models spread across the industry, a company called Musubi has a new idea for how to put them to work: moderating content. On Tuesday, Musubi announced a lightweight decision model made for real-time moderation called PolicyLM-1.7B, released with open weights.

The idea is to take a content policy written in plain English and apply it to messages in under 50 milliseconds. Musubi’s model is designed to be similar in cost and speed to the AI classifier systems that power moderation on most social platforms — but because it has the flexibility of a modern LLM, it can apply complex policies without special training. Even more important, the model won’t need new training when the policy changes, allowing for human policy-setters to iterate as much as they need.

As Musubi co-founder and chief AI officer Filip Jankovic sees it, it gives platform managers a way to label content proactively.

“Product teams just want a better understanding of what’s happening on their platform, especially as the amount of content is exponentially increasing,” Jankovic says. “Being able to label all of that in a very scalable, customizable way is extremely useful.”

Decision models have become a hot topic in the AI world since the release of TypeSafe AI’s Jev in September, which was shortly followed by competing decision models from OpenAI and Amazon. Instead of outputting text, a decision model outputs outcome probabilities, though in this case the model outputs a binary judgement: Either the content is in the category or it isn’t. By limiting the model’s output to a set of predetermined choices, decision models are able to run faster and cheaper than large language models, while still maintaining the flexibility of the transformer architecture.

One early use case is reining in misbehavior by AI agents — so it’s only natural to apply the same technology to human misbehavior.

Notably, Jankovic says his interest in decision models predates Jev, tracing it back to a 2024 project called GLiNER (Generalist Model for Named Entity Recognition) that deployed many of the same techniques.

Still, Musubi isn’t wary of the comparison. If anything, the company is eager to use the new interest in decision models to shine a light on content moderation. “If Jev caught your eye, PolicyLM-1.7B is the same kind of model, trained specifically for content moderation, that you can run yourself,” the product announcement reads.

其核心思路是获取用通俗英文编写的内容政策，并在不到50毫秒内将其应用于消息审核。Musubi的模型在成本和速度上力求与目前支撑多数社交平台审核的AI分类器系统相当——但由于它具备现代大语言模型（LLM）的灵活性，无需专门训练即可应用复杂规则。更重要的是，当政策调整时，该模型无需重新训练，从而允许人类规则制定者根据需要随时迭代。

正如Musubi联合创始人兼首席人工智能官菲利普·扬科维奇（Filip Jankovic）所看重的那样，它为平台管理者提供了一种主动标记内容的方法。

“产品团队只是希望更好地了解自己平台上正在发生的事情，尤其是在内容呈指数级增长的情况下，”扬科维奇表示，“能够以极具可扩展性、可定制化的方式对所有这些内容进行标记，是非常有价值的。”

自TypeSafe AI于9月发布Jev以来，决策模型已成为AI领域的热门话题，紧随其后的是来自OpenAI和亚马逊的同类竞争模型。与直接输出文本不同，决策模型输出的是结果概率，尽管在此场景下该模型输出的是二元判定：内容要么符合该类别，要么不符合。通过将模型的输出限定在一组预定选项内，决策模型能够以比大语言模型更快、更廉价的方式运行，同时仍保留了Transformer架构的灵活性。

一个早期的应用案例是遏制AI智能体的违规行为——因此，将相同的技术应用于人类违规行为也就顺理成章了。

值得一提的是，扬科维奇表示他对决策模型的兴趣早于Jev，可以追溯到2024年一个名为GLiNER（通用命名实体识别模型）的项目，该项目运用了许多相同的技术。

尽管如此，Musubi并不介意这种对比。甚至可以说，该公司渴望借着外界对决策模型的新兴趣，让内容审核领域受到更多关注。“如果你被Jev吸引，PolicyLM-1.7B就是同类型模型，且专门针对内容审核进行了训练，你可以自行运行它，”产品公告中写道。

aiStories.title: AI算力初创公司Lambda拟在计划IPO前融资40亿美元
aiStories.originalTitle: AI computing startup Lambda to raise $4B ahead of planned IPO
aiStories.snippet: Nvidia-backed Lambda is raising up to $4 billion at a $14.5 billion pre-money valuation ahead of a planned 2027 IPO, led by Coatue and Blackstone.
aiStories.fullContent:
Cloud provider Lambda is raising up to $4 billion at a $14.5 billion pre-money valuation, marking what could be its last private round before a planned 2027 IPO, according to The Wall Street Journal. Coatue Management and Blackstone are leading the round.

A letter to investors reviewed by the Journal shows Lambda’s backlog grew from $15 billion in June to $50 billion in September. While that might look like a hearty increase in demand, much of that increase appears to be driven by a $35 billion commitment from one company: Anthropic, which signed a deal with Lambda in late August.

That means Lambda’s valuation, which has climbed significantly since its 2025 funding round, could be leaning heavily on Anthropic’s ability to keep paying. Still, with reliable GPU capacity so scarce, investors are clearly still willing to bet on companies that provide it, especially ones with large contracts with a major AI lab.

For neoclouds like Lambda, demand isn’t so much the problem as is the cost of meeting it. Data center buildouts are largely funded by debt — of which Lambda just raised an additional $1 billion last week — and lenders are getting choosier about who they offer cash to and under what circumstances. Lambda’s decision to raise more now not only sets the tone for its IPO pricing, but also gives it access to more capital before the scrutiny of public markets arrives.

If and when Lambda does IPO — the company was reportedly meant to debut this year, but has pushed that back amid market uncertainty — it will join other Nvidia-backed neoclouds, like CoreWeave and Nebius, that now depend on the health of their stock to fund their data center buildouts. British neocloud Nscale filed for an IPO last month and is expected to begin trading soon.

Lambda, Coatue, and Blackstone did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

aiStories.fullContent:
Calling something “last-gen” usually means it comes with big compromises compared to the latest version. That’s not as true for the last-gen Kindle Paperwhite as it is with some other tech. The newer version can open books 30 percent faster (not the same as page-turning speed), and its aluminum design is a millimeter thinner — but it costs $50 more .

The 2024 edition has the same fantastic 300ppi screen, an auto-adjusting front light, and waterproof (IPX8) design. And the Signature Edition that’s discounted has no lockscreen ads, twice the storage (32GB) of the base model, plus wireless charging and an ambient light sensor, and it’s down to $169.99 (originally $249.99) at Amazon .

Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition

The premium Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition offers the same design and performance as the standard model but with more storage and support for wireless charging.

$249.99 $169.99 at Amazon

$249.99 $169.99 at Best Buy

$249.99 $169.99 at Target

The standard Paperwhite is $149.99 (was $199.99) at Amazon , and while the lower price is nice, I’d suggest only opting for that model if you’re alright with what you’re giving up (which is a lot): it has half the storage, no wireless charging, and lockscreen ads.

2024 款机型同样配备了出色的 300ppi 屏幕、自动调节的前阅读灯以及防水（IPX8）设计。而此次打折的签名版（Signature Edition）没有锁屏广告，存储容量是基础款的两倍（32GB），并支持无线充电和环境光传感器，在亚马逊的售价已降至 169.99 美元（原价 249.99 美元）。

高端的 Kindle Paperwhite 签名版提供了与标准机型相同的设计和性能，但拥有更大的存储空间并支持无线充电。

aiStories.originalTitle: EmbeddingGemma 2: an open, lightweight multimodal embedding model
aiStories.fullContent:
EmbeddingGemma 2 is the most capable model for on-device multimodal embeddings, natively mapping combinations of text, images, audio, and video into a unified embedding space.

Research Engineer, Google DeepMind

Henrique Schechter Vera

Your browser does not support the audio element.

We introduced EmbeddingGemma last year to provide a lightweight option for high-quality text embeddings, to help your apps organize, search, and connect information directly on consumer hardware. The developer community’s response blew past our expectations. With more than 20 million downloads, builders have used it to power smarter on-device search tools and privacy-first retrieval augmented generation (RAG) pipelines.Today, we’re launching EmbeddingGemma 2, expanding beyond text to unify code, images, video, and audio in a shared embedding space. Built on the Gemma 4 architecture and released under a commercially permissive Apache 2.0 license, EmbeddingGemma 2 has 740 million parameters, making it optimal for on-device inference. It can help find a specific video clip from a voice memo, or search through hours of audio recordings based on a text query, all processed by a single, natively multimodal model.

Built from the same technology as Gemini Embedding models, EmbeddingGemma 2 is:Best-in-class for its size: Achieves leading scores among sub-1B multimodal embedders for its size across benchmarks like MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) Code and MAEB (Massive Audio Embedding Benchmark), while matching or outperforming many larger models across text, vision, and audio tasks.Modular by design: Requires as little as 270M parameters for text-only workloads with optional vision (170M) and audio (300M) encoders for full multimodal support.Storage-efficient: Using Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), developers can dynamically truncate output vectors from 768 dimensions down to 512, 256, or 128 dimensions. This provides up to 6x storage reduction for local vector databases and memory usage.Optimized for on-device performance: Runs efficiently within tight resource constraints. With quantization, on a Google Pixel 11 Pro, EmbeddingGemma 2 requires as little as ~191MB active RAM for text-only weights and ~567MB for the full multimodal model.Extended context ready: Features an 8K token context window (4x larger than EmbeddingGemma 1), allowing it to process up to 5.5 minutes of audio, 29 images, 58 video frames, or interleaved combinations thereof directly on local hardware.

Across image, video, documents, and audio, it sets a new standard in quality-per-parameter for sub-1B models and even outperforms some specialist models more than twice its size.

基于与 Gemini 嵌入模型相同的技术构建，EmbeddingGemma 2 具备以下特性：同级别尺寸中表现最佳：在 MTEB（大规模文本嵌入基准）代码任务和 MAEB（大规模音频嵌入基准）等评测基准中，其表现位居 10 亿参数（sub-1B）以下多模态嵌入模型前列，并在文本、视觉和音频任务上媲美甚至超越了许多更大尺寸的模型。模块化设计：纯文本任务仅需 2.7 亿（270M）参数，同时配备可选的视觉（1.7 亿参数）和音频（3 亿参数）编码器，以实现完整的多模态支持。存储高效：采用套娃式表征学习（Matryoshka Representation Learning，简称 MRL），开发者可以将输出向量维度从 768 维动态截断至 512、256 或 128 维。这使得本地向量数据库和内存占用的存储空间最高可减少至原有的六分之一。针对端侧性能进行了优化：在严苛的资源限制下仍能高效运行。经过量化后，在 Google Pixel 11 Pro 上，EmbeddingGemma 2 的纯文本权重仅需约 191MB 的活动内存（RAM），完整多模态模型仅需约 567MB。支持扩展上下文：具备 8K token 的上下文窗口（是 EmbeddingGemma 1 的 4 倍），支持直接在本地硬件上处理长达 5.5 分钟的音频、29 张图像、58 帧视频，或这些模态的交错组合。
基于与 Gemini 嵌入模型相同的技术构建，EmbeddingGemma 2 具备：
在代码、视觉和音频上实现顶尖质量
EmbeddingGemma 2 在保持 EmbeddingGemma 强大的多语言文本性能的同时，在代码性能上实现了 9.92 分的显著提升（在 MTEB 代码评测中，从 68.76 分跃升至 78.68 分），非常适合本地代码库索引、语义化代码搜索和编码智能体检索。在图像、视频、文档和音频方面，它在 10 亿参数以下模型中树立了单位参数质量的新标杆，甚至超越了某些体积为其两倍以上的专用模型。
EmbeddingGemma 2 在保持 EmbeddingGemma 强大的多语言文本性能的同时，在代码性能上实现了 9.92 分的显著提升（在 MTEB 代码评测中，从 68.76 分跃升至 78.68 分），非常适合本地代码库索引、语义化代码搜索和编码智能体检索。在图像、视频、文档和音频方面，它在 10 亿参数以下模型中树立了单位参数质量的新标杆，甚至超越了某些体积为其两倍以上的专用模型。
完整评估指标和模型信息请参见 EmbeddingGemma 2 模型说明卡（model card）。
完全在端侧实现语义搜索、路由与检索
EmbeddingGemma 2 将强大的能力直接带到边缘硬件设备。在本地生成嵌入有助于确保数据隐私、降低工作流延迟，并赋能开发者构建完全脱机运行的跨模态搜索与检索系统。当与 Gemma 4 等生成式模型配合使用时，EmbeddingGemma 2 能够支持理解复杂多模态数据的端侧 RAG 工作流。由于 EmbeddingGemma 2 基于 Gemma 4 构建，并共享其文本分词器和音频编码器，开发者可以在统一的工作流中同时运行这两个模型，从而降低整体内存占用。
EmbeddingGemma 2 将强大的能力直接带到边缘硬件设备。在本地生成嵌入有助于确保数据隐私、降低工作流延迟，并赋能开发者构建完全脱机运行的跨模态搜索与检索系统。
当与 Gemma 4 等生成式模型配合使用时，EmbeddingGemma 2 能够支持理解复杂多模态数据的端侧 RAG 工作流。由于 EmbeddingGemma 2 基于 Gemma 4 构建，并共享其文本分词器和音频编码器，开发者可以在统一的工作流中同时运行这两个模型，从而降低整体内存占用。
使用文本或图像，根据语义相似度在媒体库中查找最匹配的内容。可在 Google AI Edge Gallery 的“即时媒体搜索”（Instant Media Search）中体验。
使用文本或音频查询在视频中定位特定时刻。可在 Google AI Edge Gallery 的“视频时刻查找器”（Video Moments Finder）中体验。
将 EmbeddingGemma 2 用于本地文件检索，与 Gemma 4 结合用于上下文推理。可在 Google AI Edge Foresight 应用程序中体验。
通过 MediaPipe 决策任务 API（Decision Task API），利用多模态上下文创建具备分类、路由和预测功能的实时决策引擎。
如需了解如何使用 LiteRT 构建端侧搜索与 RAG 系统，请参阅 Google AI Edge 官方博客文章。

上手使用 EmbeddingGemma 2
我们与以下合作伙伴紧密合作，以确保 EmbeddingGemma 2 能够直接在您的构建环境中开箱即用：
下载模型：可在 Hugging Face 和 Kaggle 上获取模型权重，且即将在 Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Model Garden 上线。访问 Hugging Face 上的 LiteRT Community 获取针对端侧优化的模型。
端侧部署：利用 Google AI Edge MediaPipe 开发跨平台应用，实现开箱即用的嵌入、检索与决策任务，或使用 LiteRT 进行自定义模型集成。亦可借助 transformers.js 或 WebGPU 面向浏览器进行构建。
使用您偏好的开发工具：使用 transformers、sentence-transformers、MLX、vLLM、llama.cpp、SGLang、Ollama 和 LMStudio 高效部署和提供模型服务。使用 Qdrant 存储您的嵌入向量。
微调：参考 Unsloth 提供的指南，了解如何针对您的业务场景对 EmbeddingGemma 2 进行微调。
探索我们的开发者指南、文档以及推理和微调指南。

aiStories.fullContent:
The MacBook Air laptops are among the discounted Apple products. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

Amazon’s October Big Deal Days are underway (lasting through tomorrow night), and we spotted a ton of Apple products and accessories in the sale, ranging from laptops and headphones to desktops and more. Some of the deals are only for Prime members , but other retailers are often matching or beating Amazon’s prices, and we’ll continue to update our coverage as we spot those deals.

If your sights are set beyond what Apple makes, our main roundup has over 100 of the best deals from October Prime Day, and we’re keeping it updated throughout the sale.

The iPhone Air is Apple’s thinnest iPhone yet at 5.6mm, featuring a 6.5-inch ProMotion display, a 48MP fusion camera, and an 18MP front camera with Center Stage support. But its single rear camera and “meh” battery life mean it’s not for everyone.

$999.99 $839.99 at Best Buy (256GB)

The iPhone 16E is the spiritual successor to the iPhone SE, bringing flagship-level performance for less than the standard 16. We really wish it included MagSafe for $599, but those upgrading from older iPhones will probably be satisfied with what’s included.

$599.99 $489.99 at Best Buy (128GB)

Apple AirPods Max (second-gen)

Apple’s second-generation AirPods Max have excellent sound and ANC performance, but are only a minor upgrade from the older pair. Read our review .

$549 $429 at Best Buy

Apple 13-inch MacBook Air (M5)

Powered by Apple’s new M5 chip, the latest MacBook Airs are more powerful than prior models and offer double the base storage (512GB). They also support faster wireless standards, specifically Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Read our review .

$1299 $1099 at Amazon

$1299 $1099 at Best Buy

Apple MacBook Air (15-inch, M5, 2026)

The 15-inch Apple MacBook Air features improved performance and better connectivity than the previous generation, and better speakers than the 13-inch model.

$1499 $1299 at Amazon

$1499 $1299 at Best Buy

The seventh-gen iPad Mini comes with Apple’s A17 Pro chip and support for Apple Intelligence. It’s also compatible with the Apple Pencil Pro and offers faster Wi-Fi and USB-C speeds. Read our review .

$599 $499 at Amazon (128GB, Wi-Fi)

$699 $599 at Amazon (256GB, Wi-Fi)

Belkin MagSafe 15W 2-in-1 wireless charging dock

A slick 2-in-1 charger that can charge your magnet-friendly iPhone or Pixel at a relatively speedy pace. Its extra charging pad supports AirPods, the Apple Watch, and other Qi-ready accessories.

$120 $59.99 at Amazon

Belkin Qi2.2 25W 2-in-1 foldable charging dock

Slap a recent iPhone onto this charging pad and it’ll charge at fast 25W speeds. It can also charge AirPods, and includes a cord and wall adapter.

$100 $75 at Amazon (w/ Apple Watch support)

The Apple Watch SE 3 is a major glow-up, adding an always-on display, wrist-temperature sensor, a more powerful processor, and fast charging. Read our review.

The AirPods Pro 3 have a new design that improves their fit, superior noise cancellation, better bass, and fairly accurate heart rate sensors. Read our review .

$249 $179.99 at Best Buy

The M4-powered iPad Air excels at AI-powered tasks, and has great battery life, but the 60Hz screen feels underwhelming. Read our review .

$749 $649 at Amazon (128GB, Wi-Fi)

$749 $649 at Best Buy (128GB, Wi-Fi)

Apple’s entry-level iPad is an excellent tablet for casual use, even if it is getting a little long in the tooth. Its high-res screen is great for watching video, and its A16 processor is still fast enough to handle light games and productivity apps. Read our review .

$449 $399 at Amazon (128GB, Wi-Fi)

Apple’s recently-updated Mac Mini packs surprising performance into a small package, and the discount helps offset a generational price bump. Read our review .

Apple Watch Series 12

The newest generation of Apple Watch packs in a variety of upgrades, like faster charging and updated sensors, alongside new Siri and AI features. Read our review .

$399 $349.99 at Amazon (42mm, GPS)

Apple’s AirPods 4 are last-gen wireless earbuds, but they’re still great. The hard, plastic buds feature improved audio over the third-gen model, along with deep iOS integration and spatial audio with head tracking. Read our review .

Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max TechWoven Case with MagSafe

This Apple iPhone case features a woven fabric made from recycled polyester for a unique look and rugged protection.

$59 $50.99 at Best Buy

The Apple Pencil Pro arrives with new features like Find My support so you can find the stylus when it gets lost, as well as new creative capabilities like squeeze gestures and the “Barrel Roll” gyroscope.

Apple Magic Keyboard Folio for iPad (A16)

This keyboard for the iPad turns your tablet into a tiny laptop, and is detachable in case you’d rather just use the kickstand folio cover.

$249 $199 at Best Buy

Speck Presidio2 Grip Case with MagSafe for Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone 17 Pro Max

This Speck case features specially designed grips that help prevent accidental drops, and is made from 50 percent recycled plastic.

$44.99 $35.99 at Best Buy

Casetify Force Case for Apple iPhone 18 Pro and 17 Pro

The Force Case from Casetify comes in a handful of trendy colors, and supports MagSafe accessories and chargers.

trendStories.title: OpenAI 公开数学研究成果目录
trendStories.fullContent:
This repository contains mathematical manuscripts and supporting proof artifacts produced by an internal OpenAI model.

As part of model development, we evaluate our models on open research problems. We expanded these evaluations after performance on our existing mathematical evaluations saturated. Some outputs build upon earlier results produced by the models.

This collection includes results at different stages of verification. Not all have accompanying Lean formalizations. We will continue to update this repository with Lean formalizations as we obtain them.

Some of the unformalized results could have issues. We will endeavor to fix any such issues quickly. We are also exploring community-hosted repositories for these materials.

The current catalogue contains 722 manuscripts organized into 372 families. A family groups related papers, which may include a principal result, companion arguments, consequences, or alternative proofs. Each family is classified by mathematical discipline.

We are also releasing abridged summaries of the model's reasoning, covering the following results:

The vast majority of results were obtained with the same procedure using an unreleased internal OpenAI model. On average, each result used three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute with that model. Over the course of the evaluation, the model was posed approximately 4,000 problems. Aggregating the output into result families and manuscripts and requiring an appropriate level of significance led to the catalog outlined above.

Exceptions to this fixed procedure include work on a zero-free region for the Riemann zeta function and proof of the Hodge Conjecture for CM abelian varieties. Additionally, the writeup for the Re(s) > 11/12 zero-free region for the Riemann zeta function was human edited for readability.

We will preserve the public release history of this collection. Corrections and revisions will be recorded as new versions, with previously released versions remaining accessible.

To cite the individual manuscript, use the BibTeX block in its directory.
trendStories.fullTranslation:
本仓库包含由 OpenAI 内部模型生成的数学论文手稿及辅助证明材料。

作为模型研发工作的一部分，我们在开放式研究问题上对模型进行了评测。在我们现有的数学基准评测表现达到饱和后，我们扩大了这些评测的范围。部分产出建立在模型先前生成的成果之上。

该合集包含处于不同验证阶段的成果。并非所有成果都附带 Lean 形式化证明。随着我们获得相应的 Lean 形式化成果，我们将持续更新此仓库。

部分尚未形式化的成果可能存在纰漏。我们将努力尽快修复任何此类问题。我们同时也在探索为这些材料设立社区托管的存储库。

当前目录包含 722 篇论文手稿，划分为 372 个成果族（families）。一个成果族将相关论文归并在一起，其中可能包含一项主要成果、配套论证、推论或替代证明。每个成果族均按数学学科门类进行了分类。

我们还发布了模型推理过程的精简摘要，涵盖以下成果：

绝大多数成果均采用相同流程、利用 OpenAI 尚未发布的内部模型获得。平均而言，针对该模型，每个成果耗费了 3 小时的 ChatGPT Pro 思考算力（thinking compute）。在整个评测过程中，模型被提出了大约 4,000 个问题。将输出聚合为成果族和手稿，并筛选出具备相应显著性水平的内容后，便形成了上文所列的目录。

该固定流程的例外情况包括：关于黎曼 zeta 函数无零点区域的研究，以及 CM 阿贝尔簇霍奇猜想（Hodge Conjecture for CM abelian varieties）的证明。此外，关于黎曼 zeta 函数 Re(s) > 11/12 无零点区域的手稿经过了人工编辑以提高可读性。

我们将保留该合集的公开发布历史。更正和修订将记录为新版本，此前发布的版本仍将保持可访问状态。

如需引用单篇论文手稿，请使用其目录下的 BibTeX 代码块。

trendStories.title: Python 3.15 到底有多快？
trendStories.fullContent:
It's October once again, and that means it is time to take the new release of Python for a spin (technically, it is the 3.15.0rc3 release that I'm using, the official 3.15 release is still a few days out). As I did with my Python 3.14 performance article of a year ago, today I'm sharing a new run of my informal Python benchmark, comparing Python 3.15 against previous interpreters all the way back to 3.10.

If you are not interested in the charts and the tables and just want to read my analysis, feel free to jump to the conclusions section at the end.

I just called my benchmark "informal". What does that mean?

Getting an objective and universal measure of the performance of a programming language is impossible. All you can do is write some programs and run them to get a measure of their performance. Other programs may show similar performance characteristics or they may not, there is really no way to know. My intention with this benchmark is just to get a feel for the performance changes across versions of Python, but I want to make it clear that I'm not trying to obtain a comprehensive performance profile of the Python interpreter.

For my benchmark I will be running two programs called fibo.py and bubble.py, which you can inspect if you like. These are the same programs I used in past editions of this benchmark. The first calculates numbers from the Fibonacci sequence, and the second sorts numbers using the bubble sort algorithm.

I've chosen these two programs as representative of two classes of algorithms. The Fibonacci calculation is done using recursion, which I have found to be somewhat inefficient in Python interpreters. On the other side, the bubble sort only uses for-loops, without any recursion. There are other types of programs that my benchmark does not attempt to cover. In particular, note that I'm not including I/O bound code in this benchmark.

Because some of the performance improvements in recent Python versions revolve around multi-threading, I also created a multi-threaded variation for each program, so in total I have four different tests.

The complete testing matrix is actually fairly complex, because I have to run the four program variations under all the Python versions, plus the JIT and free-threading alternatives for those that have them. I like to run the tests under PyPy as well, because this interpreter has shown impressive performance in past runs of this benchmark. And to place Python performance within the wider ecosystem, I've also ported the two programs to JavaScript (Node.js) and Rust.

Here is the full test matrix that I've worked with:

Readers of my previous benchmarks may recall that I had an additional dimension in my matrix for Linux vs. macOS. Given that there were no significant differences between them in the two previous runs of the benchmark, I've decided to drop the macOS tests this time around, so all tests were executed on my Linux laptop, which has an Intel Core i5 CPU and runs Gentoo Linux.

The method I'm using to measure the performance of each participant in this benchmark is to run the test program three times and take the average duration of the three. In the tables of results that I share below I also show the speed difference versus the 3.15 version, and when it makes sense also the speed difference versus the previous version of a given interpreter. For speed comparisons I'm using a simple ratio, where 1x means same speed, 0.5x means half speed (or that it took twice the time to run), 2x means twice as fast (or that it ran in half the time if you prefer), etc. Hopefully this makes sense.

Let's get started. The first test calculates the first 40 Fibonacci numbers.

Below you can see the above speeds in chart form:

From these results we can infer that for this test Python 3.15 is just a tiny bit faster than 3.14, probably not enough to matter. As I have also observed in previous years, the performance of PyPy 3.12 is out of this world, clocking in at 5.5x the speed of 3.15, and even getting a small lead over Node.js. As for Rust there are no surprises, but it is always good to know where the limits are!

Comparing each Python release against the previous one shows an interesting detail. The only two releases that made significant performance improvements over their predecessors are Python 3.11 and 3.14. You can see this clearly in the chart, when there is a larger drop in the height of a bar compared to the previous one. The other releases either maintained the same speed or made small improvements, so overall there's always been progress.

In the next set of results you can see the progress of the JIT and free-threading (FT) releases of Python on the same test. Keep in mind that these alternative versions of the Python interpreter were first introduced in 3.13, so the range of versions to evaluate is much smaller.

Below is a chart with these results:

Really the most interesting thing from this is that the JIT in the 3.15 interpreter was faster than the standard interpreter of the same test, which was not the case in previous years. And a 1.20x speed increase is not negligible, this is very exciting to see!

On the free-threading front there isn't really a lot to expect because this test is single-threaded. But we can say that the performance of the free-threading interpreter is about the same as the 3.14 one.

Let's look at the second test now. Here are the table and the chart for the single-threaded bubble sort test, which was configured to sort 10,000 random numbers:

As in the previous test, here we can also see that 3.15 had a very small improvement in performance with respect to 3.14. And we again can see that 3.11 and 3.14 are the two recent releases of Python that have really moved the needle in terms of performance. Some releases are even showing small regressions on this test. PyPy continued to be very fast, but for this test Node.js was faster.

The next table and chart show the results for the JIT and free-threading editions of the Python interpreter:

This shows the same overall picture from the first test. The 3.15 JIT once again shows an impressive 1.28x speed gain over the regular interpreter. The free-threading version shows a performance drop with respect to the standard interpreter, but a similar drop occurred with the 3.14 interpreter, so this is not a regression. As I said before, this does not matter much because this test is single-threaded, so it isn't the kind of application that will ever help the free-threading interpreter shine. I think it is reasonable to expect the free-threading interpreter to perform comparably to the regular one, so from that point of view we can say that there is work to be done yet.

Let's now repeat all the tests, but running 4 threads in parallel. Given that this is a very specific test that is designed to evaluate the free-threading version of the Python interpreter, I'm dropping the non-Python runs.

To get a baseline, first I ran the multi-threaded test on the standard Pythons. To be absolutely clear, these results are going to be bad for CPython, because the global interpreter lock (GIL) prevents true concurrency between threads. Here are the results and chart for the multi-threaded Fibonacci test:

This test shows 3.15 being a tiny bit slower than 3.14. We've seen in the single-threaded tests that the 3.15 interpreter was only slightly faster than 3.14, so overall I think we can say that the standard interpreter is about the same speed as 3.14. Here we can also see that PyPy continues to run circles around standard Python, but with the threads its speed slowed it down by a similar ratio, because PyPy's concurrency is also affected by a GIL.

Now let's see how the JIT and free-threading versions of the Python interpreters do on this test.

The free-threading edition of the Python 3.15 interpreter runs about 4.5 times faster than the standard interpreter, and the ratio was about the same with 3.14. This significant speed gain can be attributed to the interpreter running without the GIL, which allows for more efficient thread concurrency.

A secondary observation that we can make from these results is that the JIT edition of the interpreter, which runs with the GIL, keeps a similar edge over the standard interpreter even when running multiple threads, and this is new with 3.15.

We have one more set of results to go over. Here are the standard interpreter results for the bubble sort test:

This is, again, more or less in alignment with the previous results, with the 3.15 interpreter just a hair faster than 3.14.

Now that we have the baseline for this test, let's have a look at the JIT and free-threading interpreters:

And here the free-threading 3.15 interpreter is once again faster than the standard one. The gains are not as impressive as in the Fibonacci test, but this type of program is still a good use case for a GIL-free interpreter.

As for the JIT results, they seem consistent with all other runs of this interpreter, which show a great improvement in 3.15.

I hope you enjoyed looking at my benchmark. Maybe in addition to seeing a bunch of numbers and colorful charts, you are wondering what does this all mean in practical terms.

What I want to do before ending this article is to give you my personal interpretation of what these numbers suggest, because you may want to know if it makes sense to upgrade to 3.15, and what improvements you can expect to see when you do. In this section we are leaving determinism and enter opinion territory, so please keep in mind that someone else looking at these numbers may have a completely different interpretation than mine!

With the disclaimer out of the way, I'll say that my gut feeling after running the tests is that Python 3.15 is at best a fairly minor improvement over 3.14 in terms of performance. I may eventually upgrade production projects I currently have on 3.14 such as this website, but the results that I obtained do not make me want to rush an upgrade like I did after seeing such great results with 3.14 last year.

The only area where there is a clear improvement in the 3.15 release is in the JIT. But the JIT continues to be an experimental feature, so it is not a good idea to use it in production. I will consider using the JIT in production only when it is out of the experimental phase.

Aside from the JIT, there aren't really any significant performance gains in this release. Some tests do show a small performance increment, but others show regressions, so I don't expect these small variations to translate into noticeable performance changes for a real world project. I honestly don't feel I'm losing anything by staying on 3.14 for a few more months, or even until 3.16 drops in a year and I have one more release to evaluate.

I do, however, plan to use 3.15 as my main day-to-day interpreter, and maybe I will end up upgrading some of my production projects just so that I can use some of the new features, such as the JavaScript-like unpacking of comprehensions or the lazy imports.

Thank you for visiting my blog! If you enjoyed this article, please consider supporting my work and keeping me caffeinated with a small one-time donation through Buy me a coffee. Thanks!

If you like my MicroPython tutorial series on this blog, you may also like my MicroPython for the Raspberry Pi Pico W book.

I'm a software engineer and technical writer, currently living in Drogheda, Ireland.

Generative AI notice: I do not use LLMs, agents or any other generative AI tools for help with writing, coding, image creation or any other tasks related to this blog or my open source work.

You can also find me on Github, LinkedIn, Bluesky, Mastodon, Twitter, YouTube, Buy Me a Coffee, and Patreon.

Thank you for visiting!
trendStories.fullTranslation:
又到十月了，这也意味着是时候体验一下 Python 的最新版本了（严格来说，我使用的是 3.15.0rc3 版本，官方的 3.15 正式版还有几天才会发布）。正如一年前我写的 Python 3.14 性能文章一样，今天我将分享新一轮非正式的 Python 基准测试结果，对比 Python 3.15 与自 3.10 以来历代解释器的表现。

如果你对图表和表格不感兴趣，只想阅读分析内容，可以随时跳到文末的结论部分。

我刚才把我的基准测试称为“非正式”。这是什么意思呢？

要想对一门编程语言的性能得出客观且通用的衡量标准是不可能的。你所能做的只是写一些程序并运行它们，以获取其性能的度量。其他程序可能会展现出相似的性能特征，也可能不会，这真的无从得知。我做这个基准测试的初衷仅仅是想感受一下 Python 各个版本之间的性能变化，但我想明确说明的是，我并不是试图得出 Python 解释器的全面性能分析画像。

在我的基准测试中，我将运行名为 fibo.py 和 bubble.py 的两个程序，如果你愿意的话可以去查看它们。这些程序与我在此类基准测试往期版本中所使用的程序相同。第一个程序计算斐波那契数列中的数字，第二个程序使用冒泡排序算法对数字进行排序。

我选择这两个程序作为两类算法的代表。斐波那契计算使用的是递归，我发现这在 Python 解释器中效率稍显低下。另一方面，冒泡排序仅使用 for 循环，没有任何递归。还有其他类型的程序是我的基准测试并未试图涵盖的。特别是需要注意，我的基准测试中并未包含 I/O 密集型代码。

由于近期 Python 版本中的某些性能改进围绕多线程展开，因此我还为每个程序创建了一个多线程变体，所以总共有四项不同的测试。

完整的测试矩阵实际上相当复杂，因为我必须在所有 Python 版本下运行这四种程序变体，对于支持 JIT 和自由线程（free-threading）的版本还要运行其对应替代配置。我也喜欢在 PyPy 下运行这些测试，因为该解释器在此类基准测试的历史运行中展现出了令人惊艳的性能。为了将 Python 的性能置于更广阔的生态系统中进行考量，我还将这两个程序移植到了 JavaScript（Node.js）和 Rust。

以下是我使用的完整测试矩阵：

读过我以往基准测试的读者可能还记得，我的矩阵中曾包含一个 Linux 与 macOS 的额外维度。鉴于在前两次基准测试运行中两者之间并没有显著差异，这次我决定放弃 macOS 测试，因此所有测试均在一台搭载英特尔酷睿 i5 CPU 并运行 Gentoo Linux 的 Linux 笔记本电脑上执行。

我用于衡量此基准测试中每个参与者性能的方法是：将测试程序运行三次并取这三次的平均耗时。在下文分享的结果表格中，我还展示了相对于 3.15 版本的速度差异，并且在合理的情况下展示了相对于特定解释器前一版本的速度差异。对于速度比较，我使用了一个简单的比率，其中 1x 表示速度相同，0.5x 表示速度为一半（或者说花费了两倍的运行时间），2x 表示速度快一倍（或者说花费了一半的运行时间，如果你更习惯这种说法的话），依此类推。希望这能易于理解。

我们开始吧。第一项测试计算前 40 个斐波那契数。

在下方你可以看到上述速度的图表展示：

从这些结果中我们可以推断出，对于这项测试，Python 3.15 仅比 3.14 快了一点点，可能微不足道。正如我在往年观察到的那样，PyPy 3.12 的性能极为惊人，达到了 3.15 速度的 5.5 倍，甚至还略微领先于 Node.js。至于 Rust 则毫无悬念，但了解极限在哪里总是件好事！

将每个 Python 发行版与其前一版本进行对比，揭示了一个有趣的细节。唯一在性能上相较前代有显著提升的两个版本是 Python 3.11 和 3.14。你可以在图表中清楚地看到这一点，此时柱状图的高度相较前一个出现了较大幅度的下降。其他版本要么保持了相同的速度，要么带来了小幅提升，因此总体上一直是有进步的。

在下一组结果中，你可以看到 Python 的 JIT 和自由线程（FT）版本在同一测试上的进展。请记住，Python 解释器的这些替代版本最初是在 3.13 中引入的，因此可供评估的版本范围要小得多。

以下是包含这些结果的图表：

从这里来看，真正最有趣的事情是 3.15 解释器中的 JIT 比同一测试中的标准解释器更快，而在前几年情况并非如此。而且 1.20 倍的速度提升绝非微不足道，看到这一点非常令人振奋！

在自由线程方面，确实没有太多的指望，因为这项测试是单线程的。但我们可以说，自由线程解释器的性能与 3.14 版本大致持平。

现在让我们来看第二项测试。以下是单线程冒泡排序测试的表格和图表，该测试配置为对 10,000 个随机数进行排序：

与上一项测试一样，在这里我们也可以看到 3.15 相较于 3.14 只有非常微小的性能提升。我们再次看到 3.11 和 3.14 是近期真正推动了性能实质性提升的两个 Python 版本。某些版本在这项测试中甚至出现了微小的性能倒退。PyPy 依然非常快，但在本项测试中 Node.js 表现得更快。

接下来的表格和图表显示了 Python 解释器的 JIT 和自由线程版本的结果：

这展示了与第一项测试相同的总体情况。3.15 JIT 再次展现出了令人瞩目的提升，相比常规解释器获得了 1.28 倍的速度收益。自由线程版本相对于标准解释器出现了性能下滑，但 3.14 解释器也出现了类似的下滑，因此这并不算退步。正如我之前所说，这并没有太大关系，因为这项测试是单线程的，所以它并不是能让自由线程解释器大显身手的那类应用。我认为期望自由线程解释器的性能与常规解释器相当是合理的，因此从这个角度来看，我们只能说这项工作仍有待继续完善。

现在让我们并行运行 4 个线程来重复所有测试。鉴于这是一项专为评估 Python 解释器自由线程版本而设计的特定测试，我舍弃了非 Python 的运行项。

为了获得基准数据，我首先在标准 Python 版本上运行了多线程测试。需要非常明确说明的是，这些结果对 CPython 而言会比较糟糕，因为全局解释器锁（GIL）阻止了线程之间真正的并发执行。以下是多线程斐波那契测试的结果和图表：

该测试显示 3.15 比 3.14 稍微慢了一点点。我们在单线程测试中已经看到，3.15 解释器仅比 3.14 稍快一点，因此总体而言，我认为可以说标准解释器的速度与 3.14 大致相当。在这里我们还可以看到，PyPy 依然大幅领先标准 Python，但引入线程后，其速度也以类似的比例放缓，因为 PyPy 的并发同样受到 GIL 的影响。

现在让我们来看看 Python 解释器的 JIT 和自由线程（free-threading）版本在该测试中的表现。

Python 3.15 解释器的自由线程版本运行速度比标准解释器快约 4.5 倍，这一比例与 3.14 大致相同。这一显著的速度提升归功于解释器在没有 GIL 的情况下运行，从而实现了更高效的线程并发。

我们从这些结果中还可以得出第二个观察结论：在带有 GIL 的情况下运行的 JIT 版解释器，即使在运行多线程时，也对标准解释器保持着类似的优势，而这在 3.15 中是一个新现象。

我们还有一组结果需要过一遍。以下是冒泡排序测试的标准解释器结果：

这也再次与先前的结果大致吻合，3.15 解释器仅比 3.14 快一丝丝。

既然我们已经有了该测试的基准数据，接下来看看 JIT 和自由线程解释器的表现：

在这里，自由线程版 3.15 解释器再次快于标准版本。提升幅度虽然不像斐波那契测试中那么引人注目，但这种类型的程序仍然是免 GIL（GIL-free）解释器的良好使用场景。

至于 JIT 的结果，它们似乎与该解释器的所有其他运行结果一致，显示出在 3.15 中有极大的改进。

希望您喜欢我的基准测试。也许在看到一堆数字和彩色图表之余，您会好奇这一切在实际应用中意味着什么。

在结束本文之前，我想给您提供我对这些数据所代表含义的个人解读，因为您可能想知道升级到 3.15 是否合理，以及升级后可以期待看到哪些改进。在这一部分中，我们将离开确定性事实并进入观点领域，因此请记住，其他人看待这些数据可能会得出与我完全不同的解读！

免责声明交代完毕后，我想说，跑完测试后我的直觉感受是：在性能方面，Python 3.15 充其量只是对 3.14 的相当微小的改进。我可能最终会升级目前基于 3.14 的生产环境项目（例如本网站），但我获得的结果并不会让我急于升级——不像去年看到 3.14 的出色结果后那样迫切。

3.15 版本中唯一有明显改进的领域是 JIT。但 JIT 仍然是一项实验性功能，因此在生产环境中使用它并不是个好主意。只有当 JIT 脱离实验阶段后，我才会考虑在生产中使用它。

除了 JIT 之外，此版本实际上没有任何显著的性能提升。有些测试确实显示出小幅的性能提升，但其他测试却显示出性能倒退，因此我不指望这些微小的变化会转化为真实世界项目中肉眼可见的性能改变。老实说，我觉得再在 3.14 上多待几个月，甚至等到一年后 3.16 发布时再评估新版本，我也不会损失任何东西。

不过，我确实计划将 3.15 用作我日常主要使用的解释器，而且也许我最终会升级我的一些生产项目，仅仅是为了使用某些新特性，例如类似 JavaScript 的推导式解构或延迟导入（lazy imports）。

感谢您访问我的博客！如果您喜欢这篇文章，请考虑通过“Buy me a coffee”进行一次性小额赞助，以支持我的工作并让我保持充沛的咖啡因补给。谢谢！

trendStories.title: 当随机其实不够随机时
trendStories.originalTitle: When random is not actually random enough
trendStories.fullContent:
There is a common pattern you see pop up in codebases everywhere that many of us have written: given a set of objects, pick one at random. Every object should have the same chance of being picked. A rather simple and direct solution is to pick a big random number, then clamp that number to the number of choices by modulo:

I fondly remember choosing this option several times when I was much younger, especially when writing C — its standard library does not offer anything beyond rand() — and also my other language de jour, Haskell. After all, it is a fairly immediate and intuitive solution when you have such a problem, and almost any codebase or language, no matter how austere or feeble, will have some mechanism to pick a random number.

But there is a hidden problem with this solution: it doesn’t preserve the underlying uniform distribution of the given random_u64() function. That means that the variability of the chosen object you pick doesn’t respect what we might intuitively think: we might think every item has a 1/10 chance of being chosen. It does not.

Let’s start with a simpler problem: pick an integer from the interval [0, 9]. There are 10 possible picks. Assuming that our random choice function has a uniform distribution, every integer will have a chance of 1/10 = 10% of being chosen.

Then, let us use that integer to randomly pick a value from a set of 3 objects, using the modulo operator like above. The intuitive (implicit) hope is that this operation picks one of the 3 objects, each with a 1/3 = 33.3% chance; in other words, we we want the resulting probability distribution to “respect” the uniform distribution of the input variable.

Unfortunately, this is not the case; simply tabulating the outcomes makes that obvious:

In other words: of the given 10 inputs, 4 of them yield choice 1, while choice 2 and 3 only have 3 inputs that do so. This means choice 1 is picked 40% of the time rather than the intended 33%, and likewise 2 and 3 are only picked 30% of the time.

It’s one of the classic blunders, especially when random_u64() is all you have. Now, the correct behavior instead is a random_between(l, h) function which gives each inclusive number between l and h a 1/((h-l)+1) chance of being picked. Such a function is, as we might now expect, a bit more complex!

The issue in my mind is twofold. One, I think it is suboptimal API design to only offer a uniform random function, especially given that one of its most useful variants is easy to implement incorrectly. But it is also a good example of mentally working in the wrong domain in the first place.

I think the first thing is the fact that an API like random_u64() is a bit too low level and specialized. We don’t really want to sample a uniform number but a more general operator to express “how often does something happen”.

On one hand, you rarely need to only pick a random number, you normally want to pick some object out of some possible choices; second, it often is useful to weigh certain objects as more or less likely than other objects — the uniform distribution is not the only valuable one! random_u64() does not help with either of these things; a random_between(0, 9) only helps with the first at a glance (more on that shortly).

Most of the time, I think it is useful to instead reach for a more general operator, that makes you confront these issues directly: a random_choice() function that takes a set of discrete options and their probability of being chosen. In other words, you should spell out the probability distribution yourself. With this, you can represent both of the previous behaviors, and many more interesting ones.

Typically when we talk about probabilities we think of them as summing to 1.0, like the following reformulation of the original example; in such a design the erroneous “lopsided” pick is going to stick out like a sore thumb:

I think this is a case (one of many) where a generalized API, a more abstract API, can in fact make much of your code easier to reason about and write correctly too. You should of course still have random_u64() and random_between() as well — but I think random_choice() is the much better default tool because it will help you fall into the pit of success.

The previous interface is pedagogically nice but floating point instability can muddle with our ability to pick the precise weights we might need, as they must sum exactly to 1.0. Also, the requirement to sum to 1.0 is annoying as you might have to calculate the appropriate scales of each probable choice. And so when confronted with any problem involving floating point, we will use the tried and true method to handle it: get rid of it and do something else.

You will find that most standard libraries, like Python, do exactly this, with relative integer weights. The “relative” part means the numbers don’t sum to 100; instead you simply sum them and the weight of any choice is the ratio of that choice’s chance to the sum. The previous weights would be represented with (4, 3, 3) instead. 4 + 3 + 3 = 10 and so 3 / 10 = 0.3 as we expect.

One of the nice things about relative integer weights is they behave more intuitively, so you’re more likely to use it correctly. If you count the number of things in a box and see 10 blue things, and 5 red things, you can simply write out your choices at [(Blue, 10), (Red, 5)] and the resulting choice you will be distributed as you expect.

As another small note: implementing this API is much easier to do intuitively if you have random_between(l, h), not just random_u64(), which I think is another sign that random_u64() is too low level. Let’s say we have the integer weights 15 + 12 + 3 = 30. Then simply draw a random number choice = random_between(0, 29). If the chosen value is between [0, 14] it is the first option, between 15, 26 is the second option, and [27, 29] the third. In other words, you can simply map your integer weights onto to subsets of the interval [l, h] and then choosing uniformly from that interval. This is so useful and simple that it should, in my opinion, also be included with the other functions.

The other more subtle problem to me is recognizing what domain you’re operating in. In the previous examples, the things we want to talk about are not numbers, but random variables. We normally call these random variables by capital letters, X, Y, Z, etc.

Much like ordinary numbers, random variables do have an algebra to them; you can add random variables and subtract them and they feature exponents. But these operators also impact the underlying distributions and their expected outcomes, like they did here. But the most important thing is that non-linear operators do not respect the expected value of random variables. In particular, a function f over the expected value E[f(X)] is not always the same as f(E[X]).

That is what happened here; if we aren’t careful it’s easy to think we’re trying to retain some property of the value x = random_u64(), but we are actually trying to retain the properties of the underlying random_u64() function.

We are customers of Antithesis. In their platform, we effectively find bugs by exercising important code paths at random — it’s a big deterministic fuzzer, for a whole operating system. And like a fuzzer, it is useful to think about code coverage as a guiding light: “did this code get tested” is equivalent to asking “did the fuzzer find this path”, and if the fuzzer did not find that path, that code was not tested.

Increasing coverage is a matter of expressing positive and negative code paths, and then finding them under test. A negative path is a bad case that, if found, is a bug, such as an assert!() getting tripped — for instance, we might read some data from a cache, keyed by the hash of the data itself, and then assert!() that the key matches a a recomputed hash of the data.

A positive path might be ensuring that an upload function which does something different for “small” and “large” uploads actually tests both cases. In such a case, expressing your distribution directly is pretty convenient:

In this case, under test, ~7/8 uploads are small blobs of data, and ~1/8 uploads are large blobs (of three various sizes). Being able to play with these numbers is extremely valuable to help explore your state space! Extending this example to express e.g. a Poisson distribution is quite easy too.

Another useful case here I’ve found is extending the set of choices under some set of conditions; for example by using choice.push() to add something to the vector above, when some “good” or “bad” thing happens, to steer the search — this would require re-balancing the probabilities in the above example, but you can imagine structuring this example differently to avoid that.

Which leads us to this post, and something that happened last week: upon review of our Antithesis-related code recently, we ultimately were able to remove all our uses of random_u64() that had creeped in with (weighted) random_choice(), as we only ever wanted discrete weighted choices in practice anyway; we’ve put a moratorium on introducing new calls to it until further notice. I figured this lesson was important enough to not leave buried in a commit message somewhere since I keep forgetting it.

The next time you see some code like the original sample, ask yourself: can I just represent the desired distribution directly? If so you will hopefully find a much richer tool to play with!

我们在随处可见的代码库中常常能发现一个普遍的模式，而且我们许多人也曾写过这样的代码：给定一组对象，随机抽取其中一个。每个对象被抽中的概率应当相同。一个相当简单且直接的解决方案是抽取一个很大的随机数，然后通过取模将该数字限制在候选数量的范围内：

我清楚地记得，在年轻很多的时候我曾多次选择这个方案，尤其是在写 C 语言时——其标准库除了 rand() 之外没有提供任何其他东西——以及我当时常用的另一门语言 Haskell。毕竟，当面临这样一个问题时，这是一个相当直接且直观的解决方案，而且几乎任何代码库或语言，无论多么简陋或薄弱，都会有某种获取随机数的机制。

但这套解决方案存在一个隐藏的问题：它破坏了给定的 random_u64() 函数底层的均匀分布特性。这意味着所选对象的变化特征并不符合我们直觉上的设想：我们可能以为每个项目被选中的概率都是 1/10。但事实并非如此。

让我们从一个更简单的问题开始：在区间 [0, 9] 内选取一个整数。共有 10 种可能的选择。假设我们的随机选择函数具有均匀分布，那么每个整数被选中的概率均为 1/10 = 10%。

接下来，让我们像上面那样利用取模运算符，使用该整数从包含 3 个对象的集合中随机选取一个值。直觉上的（隐性）预期是该操作能以 1/3 = 33.3% 的均等概率从这 3 个对象中挑出一个；换言之，我们希望生成的概率分布能够“遵循”输入变量的均匀分布。

遗憾的是，事实并非如此；只要列出所有结果，这一点便显而易见：

换句话说：在给定的 10 个输入中，有 4 个会得到选项 1，而选项 2 和 3 分别只有 3 个输入会得出。这意味着选项 1 被选中的概率是 40%，而不是预期的 33%，同样地，选项 2 和 3 被选中的概率只有 30%。

这是最经典的错误之一，尤其是在你只有 random_u64() 可用的情况下。正确的做法应该是使用 random_between(l, h) 函数，它让 l 和 h 之间包含两端的每个数字都有 1/((h-l)+1) 的概率被选中。正如我们现在所料，这样的函数实现起来要稍显复杂一些！

在我看来，问题有两个层面。首先，我认为只提供均匀随机函数是一种次优的 API 设计，尤其是考虑到其最常用的变体很容易被错误实现。但同时，它也是从一开始就在错误的认知领域里思考的一个典型范例。

我认为首要的一点是，像 random_u64() 这样的 API 有点过于底层且过于专门化。我们真正想要的并不是对一个均匀数字进行采样，而是一个更通用的操作符，来表达“某件事发生的频率是多少”。

一方面，你很少只需要单纯抽取一个随机数，你通常想要的是从一些可能的选项中挑出某个对象；另一方面，为某些对象赋予比其他对象更高或更低的权重往往很有用——均匀分布并不是唯一有价值的分布！random_u64() 对这两点都无能为力；而 random_between(0, 9) 乍看之下也仅仅对第一点有所帮助（稍后详述）。

在大多数情况下，我认为转而使用更通用的操作符会更有帮助，它能让你直接面对这些问题：一个接收一组离散选项及其被选概率的 random_choice() 函数。换句话说，你应该亲自明确写出概率分布。有了它，你不仅可以实现之前的两种行为，还能表达许多更有趣的模式。

通常我们在讨论概率时，会认为它们的总和应为 1.0，正如对原始示例所做的如下重构；在这样的设计中，那个错误的“失衡”选取就会显得格外刺眼：

我认为这是通用 API、或者说更抽象的 API 能够切实让你大部分代码更容易推理且更易编写正确的一个案例（在众多案例中之一）。当然，你也应该保留 random_u64() 和 random_between()——但我认为 random_choice() 是好得多的默认工具，因为它会帮助你顺理成章地走向成功。

前面的接口在教学上很不错，但浮点数的不稳定性可能会干扰我们选取所需精确权重的能力，因为它们的总和必须恰好为 1.0。此外，要求总和为 1.0 也很麻烦，因为你可能不得不去计算每个可能选项的相应比例。因此，当面对任何涉及浮点数的问题时，我们会采用行之有效的方法来解决它：弃用浮点数，改用别的方式。

你会发现大多数标准库（比如 Python）正是这样做的，它们使用相对整数权重。“相对”意味着数字的总和不必为 100；你只需要将它们相加，任意选项的权重就是该选项几率与总和的比值。前面的权重可以改用 (4, 3, 3) 来表示。4 + 3 + 3 = 10，因此 3 / 10 = 0.3，正如我们所期望的那样。

相对整数权重的好处之一在于它们表现得更加符合直觉，因此你更有可能正确使用它。如果你数了一下盒子里的东西，看到有 10 个蓝色物品和 5 个红色物品，你只需将选项写为 [(Blue, 10), (Red, 5)]，最终的选取结果就会按照你的预期分布。

另外还有一个细节：如果你拥有的是 random_between(l, h) 而不仅仅是 random_u64()，直观地实现这个 API 会容易得多，我认为这再次说明了 random_u64() 过于底层。假设我们有整数权重 15 + 12 + 3 = 30。那么只需抽取一个随机数 choice = random_between(0, 29)。如果抽取的值在 [0, 14] 之间，则对应第一个选项；在 15 到 26 之间是第二个选项；[27, 29] 则是第三个选项。换言之，你可以直接将整数权重映射到区间 [l, h] 的子集上，然后从该区间内均匀抽取。这个方法既有用又简单，在我看来，它也应该与其他函数一起提供。

在我看来，另一个更为微妙的问题是弄清楚你究竟在哪个领域中进行操作。在前面的例子中，我们要讨论的并不是单纯的数字，而是随机变量。我们通常用大写字母 X、Y、Z 等来表示这些随机变量。

与普通数字非常相似，随机变量也具有代数运算性质；你可以对随机变量进行加法和减法，它们也具有指数运算。但这些运算符同样会影响底层的分布及其期望结果，正如它们在此处所表现的那样。但最重要的是，非线性运算符不遵循随机变量的期望值运算。具体而言，期望值上的函数 f，即 E[f(X)]，并不总是等同于 f(E[X])。

这里发生的情况正是如此；如果我们不加注意，就很容易误以为自己是在试图保留变量值 x = random_u64() 的某种特性，但实际上我们想要保留的是底层 random_u64() 函数本身的特性。

我们是 Antithesis 的客户。在其平台上，我们通过随机执行关键代码路径来切实有效地发现漏洞——它相当于一个面向整个操作系统的庞大确定性模糊测试工具（fuzzer）。就像模糊测试工具一样，将代码覆盖率视为指路明灯是很有用的：“这段代码是否被测试过”等同于提问“模糊测试工具是否发现了该路径”，如果模糊测试工具没有发现该路径，那么这段代码就没有被测试到。

提高覆盖率的关键在于表达正面与负面代码路径，并在测试中触发它们。负面路径是指一种异常情况，一旦触发就是漏洞，例如触发了 assert!() 报错——例如，我们可能会根据数据本身的哈希值作为键，从缓存中读取某些数据，然后断言 assert!() 该键与重新计算的数据哈希值相匹配。

正面路径则可能是确保某个在“小规模”和“大规模”上传时执行不同逻辑的上传函数，确实对这两种情况都进行了测试。在这种情况下，直接表达你的概率分布是非常方便的：

在这种情况下，在测试过程中，约 7/8 的上传是小数据块，约 1/8 的上传是大数据块（分为三种不同大小）。能够灵活调整这些数值对于帮助探索状态空间极其宝贵！将这个示例扩展到表达诸如泊松分布等分布也相当容易。

我在这里发现的另一个实用场景是在某些特定条件下扩展选项集合；例如，当发生某种“好的”或“坏的”情况时，使用 choice.push() 向上述向量中添加内容，以此来引导搜索方向——这需要重新平衡上述示例中的概率，但你可以设想通过不同的结构设计来避免这一问题。

这就引出了这篇文章，以及上周发生的一件事：最近在审查与 Antithesis 相关的代码时，我们最终彻底移除了那些悄悄混入的 random_u64() 用法，改用（带权重的）random_choice()，因为在实践中我们无论如何都只想要离散的加权选择；在另行通知之前，我们已暂停引入对其的新调用。我觉得这个教训非常重要，不能让它被埋没在某个提交信息（commit message）中，况且我自己也总是容易忘记它。

下次当你看到类似最初示例的代码时，不妨问问自己：我能否直接表达所需的分布？如果可以，你很有希望能找到一个丰富得多的工具供你使用！

trendStories.title: x32 架构下的 Janet：32 位指针、64 位速度，内存占用减少 25%
trendStories.originalTitle: Janet on x32: 32-bit Pointers, 64-bit Speed, 25% Less RAM
trendStories.fullContent:
It’s possible to save a dramatic amount of memory (close to half for programs with pointer heavy heaps) and also speed up programs by a modest amount (by way of more data fitting in cache) by using 32 bit pointers on 64 bit systems.

The Linux x32 ABI lets you do just this, but it’s tragically underused and overlooked. It’s disabled by default on Debian (though you can enable it with a boot flag) and not even compiled in on Arch Linux. Most software compiles just fine for x32, but there isn’t much packaging for it so you do have to compile nearly everything yourself.

I experimented with deploying mastodon on x32 and it cut the app’s memory usage from 650mb to 350mb. There’s so much potential here, but the work is mostly of the thankless coordination and communication type and I don’t have the time or motivation to push it forward myself. - Hailey

Janet libraries like Spork supply their own build flags, but we can hijack them with a fake cc which starts the real one with the necessary -m32 -msse2 -mfpmath=sse flags. I modified the beginning of my default Janet build script:

Easy enough! Now let’s try it!

tl;dr: 20% memory reduction, 50% slower

This is on cachyos (arch, btw) with lib32-glibc lib32-gcc-libs. Adding this to a build script forces libraires like spork to build at 32 bit too!

Note, these use Fish and I don’t want to rebuild my site with other language support:

I added a 0 in the test

For e.g. declarative-dsls/tests.janet

Unfortunately, Ubuntu also dropped x32 support.

Luckily, lazily, I have access to some deprecated servers (of course not in prod…) and OS installs, wasting hard disk space:

Ubuntu 20.04 LTS Focal Fossa has reached its end of standard support on 31 May 2025.

Ubuntu, so we have bash again:

Just what we need, although gcc version 9.4.0 is a bit old. We already have build-essential git gcc-multilib libc6-dev-x32. We’re almost ready to test this hunch. But first, we must change src/include/janet.h:

lest Janet choose the 64-bit value layout. Our build script will also pass a build flag to disable Janet’s FFI. Here is our full 32janet.sh:

And a `64janet.sh to compare it with:

Now we compare them:

But declarative-dsls is a worst case scenario, using typed c arrays for big speed ups, which don’t benefit much from this. Lets make some minimal benchmarks to really test the differences:

words.janet builds a text, splits it into words, counts them and sorts on that:

records.janet groups structs by department and summarizes those departments, with unused extra fields like real code:

parse.janet parses lines with a PEG and totals them:

tree.janet builds and walks binary trees, our pointer-heaviest example:

-mx32 cut RAM use by 21% (8-32%) with equal speed (-13% slower to 10% faster), while -x32 reduced speed by half. Janet is a worst case where nanboxing already packs values into 8 bytes so the main benefit’s smaller headers. I invite others to test their software and languages similarly. With continued x32 support, we could use this as a default for scripts, utilities, daemons and the like. I thus believe Linux distros should include -mx32 support and daemons and utilities should be compiled down for more efficient idling and day to day computing! It only costs a flag.

If Janet works with smaller object headers, why not shrink them in the implementation for 64-bit use? By my understanding, Janet heap objects use 16 bytes to help the garbage collector:

Reducing these would require a different garbage collection strategy e.g. our own allocator, which would hurt a core Janet use case: embedding in other projects.

Each type then adds:

For structs and tables in particular, we could regain 8 bytes through rearranging (not needing the later padding). Onlt tuples parsed from code need the source information (for errors); a flag could save normal tuples 8 bytes.

Unfortunately, glibc’s malloc adds 8 bytes and rounds to multiples of 16 so structs would remain the same. But tables and (some) tuples would shrunk more than the above indicates!

Kernels must be compiled with CONFIG_X86_X32_ABI providing syscall entry points on Linux (with no Windows and Mac equivalent) which the compilers expose via -mx32.
trendStories.fullTranslation:
通过在 64 位系统上使用 32 位指针，有可能大幅节省内存（对于堆中包含大量指针的程序，节省幅度接近一半），并能在一定程度上提升程序运行速度（得益于更多数据能够装入缓存）。

Linux x32 ABI 正是为此而设计的，但可惜它被严重低估且未得到充分使用。它在 Debian 上默认处于禁用状态（尽管可以通过启动标志启用），在 Arch Linux 上甚至根本没有编译进内核。大多数软件针对 x32 的编译都很顺利，但针对该架构的打包分发很少，因此几乎所有东西都需要自己编译。

我曾尝试在 x32 上部署 Mastodon，它将该应用的内存占用从 650MB 降到了 350MB。这其中蕴含着巨大的潜力，但相关工作主要是吃力不讨好的协调和沟通类事务，我自己既没有时间也没有动力去推进它。——Hailey

像 Spork 这样的 Janet 库提供了自己的构建标志，但我们可以通过一个伪装的 cc 来拦截它们，该伪装脚本会附带必需的 -m32 -msse2 -mfpmath=sse 标志来启动真实的编译器。我修改了我默认的 Janet 构建脚本的开头：

相当简单！现在让我们来试试！

太长不看版（tl;dr）：内存减少 20%，速度慢了 50%

这是在配备了 lib32-glibc 和 lib32-gcc-libs 的 CachyOS（顺便提一句，基于 Arch）上测试的。将这些添加到构建脚本中，也会强制让像 Spork 这样的库以 32 位构建！

注意，这些使用了 Fish shell，而我不想为了支持其他语言重新构建我的网站：

我在测试中添加了一个 0

例如针对 declarative-dsls/tests.janet

不幸的是，Ubuntu 也放弃了对 x32 的支持。

幸运的是，由于偷懒，我正好可以访问一些已废弃的服务器（当然不是生产环境……）和操作系统安装实例，它们正闲置浪费着硬盘空间：

Ubuntu 20.04 LTS Focal Fossa 已于 2025 年 5 月 31 日结束标准支持。

由于是 Ubuntu，我们又可以用回 bash 了：

正好满足我们的需求，尽管 gcc 9.4.0 版本有点老。我们已经拥有了 build-essential、git、gcc-multilib 和 libc6-dev-x32。我们几乎准备好验证这个直觉了。但首先，我们必须修改 src/include/janet.h：

以免 Janet 选择了 64 位的数值内存布局。我们的构建脚本还将传递一个构建标志以禁用 Janet 的 FFI。以下是我们完整的 32janet.sh：

以及用于对比的 64janet.sh：

现在我们将它们进行对比：

但 declarative-dsls 是最极端的情况，它使用有类型的 C 数组来大幅提速，因而从这种调整中获益不大。让我们制作一些最小基准测试来真正测试其差异：

words.janet 会构建一段文本，将其拆分成单词，统计词频并依此排序：

records.janet 按部门对结构体进行分组并汇总这些部门，像真实代码一样带有未使用的额外字段：

parse.janet 使用解析表达式文法（PEG）解析行并进行求和：

tree.janet 构建并遍历二叉树，这是我们测试中指针最密集的范例：

-mx32 使内存占用降低了 21%（幅度在 8% 到 32% 之间），且保持了相当的速度（从慢 13% 到快 10% 不等），而单纯的 -m32 则使速度降低了一半。Janet 属于优化潜力较小的情况，因为它的 NaN-boxing 技术已经将数值压缩到了 8 字节中，所以主要收益仅来自于更小的对象头部。我建议其他人也对其软件和语言进行类似的测试。在持续的 x32 支持下，我们可以将其作为脚本、实用工具、守护进程等程序的默认选择。因此我认为 Linux 发行版应当包含 -mx32 支持，守护进程和系统工具应该以此方式编译，从而在待机和日常计算中实现更高的能效！这只需要多加一个编译标志而已。

既然 Janet 可以在更小的对象头部下工作，为什么不在其 64 位实现中也缩减它们呢？根据我的理解，Janet 的堆对象使用 16 字节来辅助垃圾回收器：

缩减这些将需要采用不同的垃圾回收策略，例如自建分配器，但这会损害 Janet 的核心用例之一：嵌入到其他项目中。

随后每种类型会增加：

特别是对于结构体（struct）和表（table），我们可以通过重排来重新找回 8 个字节（无需后续的内存填充）。只有从代码中解析出来的元组（tuple）才需要源信息（用于报错）；一个标志位就可以让常规元组省下 8 个字节。

不幸的是，glibc 的 malloc 会增加 8 字节并按 16 的倍数对齐，因此结构体的大小将保持不变。但表和（部分）元组的缩减幅度会比上述显示的还要大！

内核必须在开启 CONFIG_X86_X32_ABI 的情况下进行编译，以便在 Linux 上提供系统调用入口点（Windows 和 Mac 没有对应支持），编译器则通过 -mx32 将其暴露出来。

trendStories.title: 用于传递程序状态的终端协议（OSC 7501）
trendStories.originalTitle: A Terminal Protocol for Program Status (OSC 7501)
trendStories.fullContent:
I wrote a specification for a new terminal escape sequence: OSC 7501, the Program Status Protocol. It lets any program tell the terminal what it's doing: idle, working, waiting on the user, finished, or failed, and why.

For example, here is how Terraform could indicate that it is blocked waiting for user input, with the message "Apply 3 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy?" (base64-encoded). A terminal (or any other tool running Terraform) could show this information however it feels appropriate: a notification, an inbox, a status icon, etc.

This post covers why I think this protocol needs to exist, why the existing approaches aren't good enough (especially for coding agents), and how the protocol works.

This is a completely generic, terminal-native specification and protocol. It emerged from my work on Superlogical and Ghostty but the specification has no product-specific functionality or language. It is designed as an idiomatic, well-formed specification that any terminal developer will find familiar.

Long-running work is common in terminals: builds, deployments, package upgrades, data processing, and, more and more today, coding agents. These programs alternate between working on their own, waiting on the user, and finishing. Meanwhile, users usually go off and do something else and want to know when the work finishes or needs them.

Aspects of this problem have been solved in various ways going back decades. For example, some terminals monitor the active foreground process and have features to notify when it changes. Or, they wait for some time period of "quiet" (for various definitions) output. The specification also lists the reasons why existing sequences aren't enough.

Ultimately, I felt there wasn't a cohesive, interaction-agnostic, generic solution to this problem that conveyed progress, blocking, completion, and trees of tasks. And it wasn't possible to cobble together pre-existing sequences to achieve it robustly, either.

Don't care about AI, LLMs, etc.? Skip this section. The problem is generic and applies in a compelling way without bringing in AI. It's particularly nasty with AI so I want to call it out, but if you don't care about any of that, just skip this.

It's now increasingly common for people to run many long-running agents for any number of reasons: background research, issue monitoring, bug fixing, large features, etc. Each one works for a while and then stops to ask for permission, ask a question, or report it's done.

From this, a new category of tool has emerged that I'll simply call the agentic inbox: a single view across every running agent showing which are working, which are done, and which are waiting on you. Herdr, cmux, and Agent Deck are a few examples of hundreds.

Without a dedicated protocol, they solve the agent status problem in two ways: heuristics and non-terminal APIs.

The first approach is to guess by reading the screen or the window title and matching it against known patterns.

Herdr is a good example because it does this well and documents it openly. Its detection manifests are TOML rules that classify an agent as idle, working, or blocked. Here is the first of 16 rules for Claude Code:

Claude Code is considered "working" if its window title starts with a Braille spinner character or, as of version 2.1.228, a half-circle one. The history of that file shows ten changes in three months for just Claude Code.

This isn't a criticism of Herdr. Its maintainers are doing the best possible job with the tools available. But it demonstrates well the benefit a unified protocol would have.

The second approach is to have the program report its own state through an inbox-specific, out-of-band API such as Herdr's socket API or cmux notify. This is better than heuristics in some ways, because the program that actually knows its state is the one reporting it. But every program has to integrate with every inbox separately, and a local socket doesn't work over SSH or from within a container without extra bridging. The pty already works across all of this.

OSC 7501 is a terminal native answer to this problem. The program reports its own state directly via the pty that it always has, using a format that is safe to send everywhere (well-behaved terminals ignore unknown OSCs).

The body of the sequence is a list of key=value pairs separated by :. The only required key is state, which is one of:

Optional keys include app, a stable machine-readable program name like cargo or claude-code, and msg, a single human-readable line encoded as base64.

Programs that run several things at once can report multiple records using hierarchical ids. A deploy tool can be working at the root while us-east pushes an image at 40% and eu-west is blocked waiting for approval to deploy to production. Both are true at the same time, and the terminal decides what to show. A clear state removes records.

Here's a complete integration for a shell script to wrap rsync to participate in this protocol:

Trivial to script with plain old POSIX sh. No SDK, no sockets, no environment variables, no JSON. No bias towards specific GUI presentations. No bias to any specific workload (like AI). A well-formed, generic foundation to build functionality above that anyone and everyone can participate with.

The full spec covers the rest: record lifetime, feature detection, terminfo, size limits, and security. It's short. I wrote it all by hand. Please read it.

I wrote this specification based on my experience maintaining a terminal emulator for many years now. It is written in a way that is easy for application developers to emit, and easy for terminal emulators to consume and parse.

I've already implemented this protocol twice. We have one implementation in libghostty and I have a parallel implementation in Rex. I've also implemented it as a proof-of-concept in Terraform, Claude Code, Codex, and Homebrew via either plugins or forks. In each case, the implementation was no more than a dozen lines.

I've been in contact with the maintainers of many popular terminal programs and emulators and they've helped review and shape the specification. But if you have any more feedback, I'm happy to hear it.

If you've implemented the specification please let me know via email (mail icon in the footer) and I'll add you to the list of tools that implement this. Thank you.

I'd like us all to stop guessing what programs are doing by reading their screens or process trees. The program already knows. Let's give it a way to tell us!
trendStories.fullTranslation:
我为一种新型终端转义序列编写了规范：OSC 7501，即“程序状态协议”（Program Status Protocol）。它允许任何程序向终端告知自己当前的状态：空闲（idle）、运行中（working）、等待用户响应（waiting on the user）、已完成（finished）或失败（failed），以及其具体原因。

例如，Terraform 可以通过该协议指示其当前正阻塞并等待用户输入，附带信息为“Apply 3 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy?”（经过 base64 编码）。终端（或任何运行 Terraform 的其他工具）都可以按其认为合适的方式展示这些信息：发送通知、收件箱式列表、状态图标等。

本文阐述了我为何认为需要存在这样一个协议、为何现有方法不够完善（特别是对于编码智能体/coding agents 而言），以及该协议的具体工作机制。

这是一个完全通用的、终端原生的规范与协议。它源于我在 Superlogical 和 Ghostty 上的工作，但该规范本身不包含任何特定于产品的功能或用语。它被设计成一个符合惯例、结构良好的规范，任何终端开发者都会感到熟悉。

长时间运行的任务在终端中屡见不鲜：构建、部署、软件包升级、数据处理，以及如今越来越常见的编码智能体。这些程序会在自行运行、等待用户以及最终完成之间交替切换。与此同时，用户通常会转去处理其他事情，并希望在工作完成或需要用户介入时收到通知。

这个问题的各个方面早在几十年前就已通过各种方式得到解决。例如，有些终端会监控活跃的前台进程，并具备在其发生变化时发出通知的功能。或者，它们会等待某段“静默”（有不同的定义）输出的时间。该规范中也列出了现有转义序列无法满足需求的具体原因。

归根结底，我认为目前尚未有一种连贯统一、与交互形式无关且通用的解决方案来传达进度、阻塞、完成以及任务树。而且，仅靠拼凑现有的转义序列也无法稳健地实现这一目标。

如果你不关心 AI、LLM 等话题，可以跳过本节。该问题属于通用范畴，即便不引入 AI，也是一个极具说服力的需求。只是在 AI 场景下该问题尤为棘手，所以我特意提出来；但如果你完全不关心这些，直接跳过即可。

如今，人们越来越频繁地出于各种原因同时运行多个长时间运行的智能体：后台调研、Issue 监控、错误修复、大型功能开发等。每一个智能体都会运行一段时间，然后停下来请求权限、提出疑问，或报告任务已完成。

由此催生了一类新工具，我统称为“智能体收件箱”（agentic inbox）：一个集中查看所有正在运行的智能体的单一视图，显示哪些正在运行、哪些已完成，以及哪些正在等待你响应。Herdr、cmux 和 Agent Deck 就是此类数百个工具中的几个代表。

在缺乏专用协议的情况下，它们主要通过两种方式解决智能体状态问题：启发式匹配（heuristics）和非终端 API。

第一种方法是通过读取屏幕内容或窗口标题，并将其与已知模式进行比对来猜测状态。

Herdr 是一个很好的范例，因为它在这方面做得不错且开源记录完备。它的检测清单采用 TOML 规则，将智能体归类为空闲、运行中或阻塞。以下是针对 Claude Code 的 16 条规则中的第一条：

如果 Claude Code 的窗口标题以盲文旋转微调字符开头，或者自 2.1.228 版本起以半圆字符开头，则被判定为“运行中”。仅针对 Claude Code，该文件的历史记录显示在三个月内就发生了十次变更。

这并非对 Herdr 的批评。其维护者已经利用现有工具做到了极致。但这也充分证明了统一协议能带来的巨大价值。

第二种方法是让程序通过特定于某个收件箱工具的带外 API 来报告自身状态，例如 Herdr 的 socket API 或 cmux notify。在某些方面这比启发式猜测更好，因为真正知晓状态的程序本身就是状态的报告者。但是，每个程序都必须单独与每个收件箱工具进行集成，而且本地 socket 在跨 SSH 或容器内部使用时，若没有额外的桥接就无法工作。而伪终端（pty）天然就能覆盖所有这些场景。

OSC 7501 是解决该问题的终端原生方案。程序直接通过始终具备的 pty 报告自身状态，使用的格式即使发送到任何地方也是安全的（规范的终端会直接忽略未知的 OSC 序列）。

该转义序列的主体是一组以冒号（:）分隔的键值对（key=value）。唯一必需的键是 state，其值为以下之一：

可选的键包括 app（一个稳定的机器可读程序名，如 cargo 或 claude-code）以及 msg（单行人类可读的消息，采用 base64 编码）。

同时运行多个任务的程序可以使用层级化 ID 报告多条记录。一个部署工具可能在根节点显示“运行中”，而 us-east 节点正在推送镜像（进度 40%），eu-west 节点则处于“阻塞”状态等待批准部署至生产环境。两者在同一时刻都成立，终端可自行决定如何呈现。clear 状态则用于移除记录。

以下是一个用于包装 rsync 以接入该协议的完整 Shell 脚本集成示例：

使用老旧朴素的 POSIX sh 就能轻而易举地编写脚本。不需要 SDK，不需要 socket，不需要环境变量，也不需要 JSON。对特定的 GUI 呈现形式没有任何偏向。对任何特定工作负载（如 AI）也没有偏见。这是一个结构良好、通用的底层基础，任何人和任何工具都能在此之上构建功能并参与其中。

完整规范涵盖了其余所有细节：记录生命周期、特性探测、terminfo、大小限制和安全性。规范很简短，全部由我亲手编写。欢迎阅读。

我结合多年维护终端模拟器的经验编写了这一规范。它的设计旨在让应用程序开发者易于输出，同时也让终端模拟器易于接收和解析。

我已经对该协议进行了两次实现。我们在 libghostty 中有一处实现，我在 Rex 中也有一份并行实现。此外，我还通过插件或分支形式，在 Terraform、Claude Code、Codex 和 Homebrew 中完成了概念验证集成。在每种情况下，实现代码均不超过十几行。

我已与许多热门终端程序和模拟器的维护者取得联系，他们帮助审阅并完善了该规范。如果你有更多反馈，我也非常乐意倾听。

如果你已经实现了该规范，请通过电子邮件告知我（页脚有邮件图标），我会将你添加到实现该协议的工具列表中。多谢。

我希望我们所有人都不再需要通过读取屏幕或进程树来猜测程序在做什么。程序本身早就一清二楚。让我们给它一个直接告诉我们的途径吧！
